newsitem.title: USA: Josephine becomes cold front over U.S. East Coast.
newsitem.headline: Josephine becomes cold front over U.S. East Coast.

text.p: Tropical Storm Josephine lost its tropical punch as it moved inland early on Tuesday, turning into a cold front that threatens heavy rain on the U.S. East Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.
Josephine drenched Florida's northern Gulf coast after coming ashore late Monday, causing widespread flooding. But there were no reports of major damage or injuries.
The storm, which never became a hurricane, continued north-east into Georgia and merged with a cold weather frontal system over the south-east of the United States.
"Josephine has lost its tropical characteristics. It has turned into a cold front," said National Hurricane Center forecaster David Chorney.
He said the storm was located 50 miles (80 km) south-east of Savannah, Georgia, at 5:30 a.m. EDT, and was continuing to move East North East at 25 miles an hour (40 kph).
Chorney said Josephine would become a gale storm, causing strong winds and heavy rain along the east seaboard. High surf would also cause beach erosion up the coast, he said.
The storm swallowed up coastal roads when it blew across Florida's northern Gulf coast on Monday night.

The Suwannee River, which snakes from southern Georgia into northern Florida, spilled out of its banks by midnight on Monday. The river, made famous by a Stephen Foster song, empties into the Gulf of Mexico.
Josephine's 65 mph (105 km) winds ripped down coastal power lines in three northern Florida counties and left most of the state soggy and windblown.
At least a dozen tornadoes skipped across northern and central Florida late on Monday, with one twister destroying trailers in Edgewater, a small community near Daytona Beach, officials said.
By midnight, the outer edge of Josephine had pushed ashore in a sparsely populated area between Apalachicola and Cross City, Florida.
Electricity was out in the coastal areas of Taylor, Dixie and Levy counties, emergency officials said.
An emergency shelter at Cross City High School, about 12 miles (20 km) inland, held two dozen evacuees from the coastal villages of Horseshoe Beach and Suwannee.

"My home is still not fixed from the 'storm of the century'," said Wanda Peters, whose Horseshoe Beach home on 12-foot (3.5 metre) stilts was flung 50 yards (45 metres) in March 1993 by the biggest storm ever to hit the area.

The 1993 unnamed "storm of the century" swept through Florida's Gulf Coast with heavy rain, killing about 20 people in flooding. As it moved north, the storm turned into a record blizzard that shut down much of the U.S. eastern seaboard.
Josephine stayed below hurricane strength, which begins with winds of at least 74 mph (118 kph).
